title: How many partitions should a topic have, what are the real constraints, and why can you never decrease partition count?
shortTitle: How many partitions should a topic have, what are the real constraints, and why can you never decrease partition count?

s1_definition.oneliner: Partitions are the parallelism dial sized by throughput with headroom, bounded by broker and latency limits, and you can only add them, never remove them, because removal would break key ordering and strand data.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partition count** -- sets the maximum consumer parallelism for a topic because within a consumer group each partition is consumed by at most one consumer.
- **Sizing formula** -- target throughput divided by per-partition throughput, with headroom for future scaling, gives the starting number.
- **Broker constraints** -- each partition replica is a set of files, so more partitions mean more open file handles, memory for indexes, slower rebalances, and longer recovery after failures.
- **Increase only** -- you can add partitions with `kafka-topics --alter` but can never decrease them, because reducing partitions would break the `hash(key) % numPartitions` mapping and strand data.
- **Over-partitioning cost** -- too many partitions hurt end-to-end latency, controller operations, and recovery time, so generous does not mean unlimited.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of partitions as the number of teller counters at National Bank of India. More counters let more tellers serve customers at once, so you size the counters to the expected rush. But there is a limit to how many counters one branch building can hold without chaos. And once you have assigned customers to counters by the first letter of their surname, you cannot suddenly remove counters, because then customers who were always served at counter five would scatter, breaking the orderly queue history you promised each customer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
 Partition Count Sizing Flow
 ===========================

 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Estimate Target Throughput  │
 │  e.g. 60 MB/s               │
 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Measure Per-Partition Rate  │
 │  e.g. 10 MB/s per consumer  │
 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Floor = 60 / 10 = 6        │
 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Add Headroom (2x) = 12     │
 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Check Broker Constraints   │
 │  - File handles             │
 │  - Memory                   │
 │  - Controller overhead      │
 │  - Rebalance time           │
 └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐
 │  Create Topic with 12       │
 │  Partitions                 │
 └─────────────────────────────┘


 Key-to-Partition Mapping
 ========================

  hash("SAV2001") = 839201

  With 6 partitions:   839201 % 6  = 3  ──► Partition 3
  With 12 partitions:  839201 % 12 = 9  ──► Partition 9

  Same key, different partition!
  Rajesh's old records: Partition 3
  Rajesh's new records: Partition 9
  Ordering broken across the split.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The partition count is the parallelism dial for a topic, because inside a consumer group each partition is read by at most one consumer, so the number of partitions is the ceiling on how many instances can consume in parallel. I size it from throughput: I take the target throughput and divide by what a single partition can sustain given the downstream processing, then I add headroom, usually doubling, so the consumer group can scale later without a repartition.

The constraints are real and I respect them. Every partition is files on a broker, so more partitions mean more open file handles and more memory for indexes and page cache. There is a practical ceiling on partitions per broker and per cluster, and too many partitions lengthen rebalances, slow controller operations, raise end-to-end latency because batches fill more slowly, and slow recovery after a broker failure. So over-partitioning to be safe is itself a cost.

You can increase partitions with an alter command, but you can never decrease them. Physically, Kafka has no safe way to merge partition logs, so shrinking would strand or require deleting data. More importantly, producers map a key to a partition by hashing the key modulo the partition count, so changing the count makes the same key map to a different partition, which breaks the guarantee that all of one key's records live in one ordered partition.

Remember one sentence: partition count caps consumer parallelism and can only increase, never decrease, because the key-to-partition hash depends on the count.

---

keyPoints: Partition count caps consumer parallelism because each partition is consumed by at most one consumer in a group.
Sizing formula is target throughput divided by per-partition throughput, with headroom typically doubled.
Constraints include open file handles, memory, rebalance time, controller overhead, and end-to-end latency.
You can increase partitions with kafka-topics --alter but can never decrease them.
Decreasing would break key-to-partition mapping because hash(key) mod numPartitions changes with the count.
Over-partitioning hurts latency, recovery time, and wastes broker resources.
For keyed topics like per-account streams, plan the partition count carefully at design time.
